newsitem.title: USA: March jobs report to set tone for Wall St stocks.
newsitem.headline: March jobs report to set tone for Wall St stocks.

text.p: The March jobs report, expected at 0830 EST/1330 GMT, will dictate the opening for Wall Street stocks Friday.
Analysts said that if the report showed little sign of wage pressure, the market could reverse and head higher after selling off in four of the last five trading sessions.
But evidence of wage pressures would trigger another selloff as it stoked fears of another Fed tightening.
The Dow industrials have fallen 608 points, or 8.6 percent, since they peaked at 7085.16 on March 11.
The U.S. non-farm payroll total is forecast to show an increase of 196,000 in March after rising by 339,000 the previous month, according to a Reuters poll of economists.
U.S. average hourly earnings, used by many participants as a guide to inflationary pressures, are expected to rise by 0.4 percent in March, after a 0.2 percent increase in February.
The unemployment rate is expected at 5.2 percent compared with 5.3 percent in February.
"Everything is predicated upon this report today," said Peter Cardillo, director of research at Westfalia Investments.

"The failure of the market to break even at the close yesterday points to the fact that there is still a lot of program selling and an unwillingness on the part of investors to step up to the plate," Cardillo said.

"If there are no real wage pressures in the report, my guess is that we will see bonds rally, and that will mean a better stock market during the day. But if there is a substantial increase in wages, we are in for an ugly day."
He said that he felt the correction in the stock market was over and would last, at worst, for a few days more if the jobs report came in stronger than expected.
In Tokyo, the Nikkei Average lost 268.72 points, or 1.48 percent, to close at 17,860.59.
In London, the FTSE 100 index was up 25.8 at 4240.4.

U.S. shares were little changed in London on Friday as participants awaited the U.S. jobs report. Intel Corp, which rose 3-5/8 in New York on Thursday, was up 1/4 at 140-7/8 while Texas Instruments Inc added 1/4 to 78-1/8. Philip Morris Cos Inc was down 3/8 at 114.
The dollar was bolstered versus the yen by comments from visiting U.S. Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin. The dollar was in a narrow range in Europe.
U.S. Treasuries were thinly mixed, with the long bond unchanged to yield 7.07 percent.

The Wall Street Journal's Heard on the Street writes that Amerindo Investment Advisors of San Francisco has been one of the top money managers in the country for the past few years. But lately, it's fallen to earth -- hard.
It said the firm was buffeted by a downdraft in the small technology stocks it loved and posted investment losses for two quarters in a row while the overall stock market advanced.

The New York Times Market Place writes that most chief executives decided to excercise few if any stock options in 1996. they passed up sure gains from the market's 1996 rise and took their chances on the ride in 1997 and beyond.
